title: Chicken Yassa, Oven-Roasted
author: Khadim Mbamba
desc: The chicken roasts at 200C for forty-five minutes while the onions cook down separately for thirty-five to forty — deep golden, then melting and caramelised.
longDesc: A chef's version that splits the work in two: four whole chicken legs, slashed and marinated, roast at 200C fan 180C for forty-five minutes until deep golden and cooked through, while four onions — two roughly chopped into the marinade and two thinly sliced — cook down for thirty-five to forty minutes until melting and caramelised. The marinade is blitzed garlic, spring onion, half a green pepper, ginger, scotch bonnet and parsley with a good pinch of salt, the juice of two lemons and a tablespoon of Dijon. The two halves come together with green olives for a final five minutes on low heat.
ingredients: 4 medium onions — 2 roughly chopped, 2 thinly sliced
1 scotch bonnet chilli, deseeded and chopped
4 whole chicken legs, skin on, slashed
steps: Blitz the roughly chopped onions, garlic, spring onion, green pepper, ginger, scotch bonnet and parsley with a good pinch of salt.
Add the lemon juice and the Dijon mustard.
Marinate the chicken with the sliced onion for at least a couple of hours, or overnight.
Roast the chicken at 200C, fan 180C, gas 6, for 45 minutes, until deep golden and cooked through.
Meanwhile cook the marinade and onions down — starting on high heat, then medium-high — for 35 to 40 minutes, until cooked through, melting and caramelised.
Add the roasted chicken and the olives, cover, and finish for 5 minutes on a low heat.
Serve with plain rice, couscous or vermicelli.
chefTips: Melting and caramelised is the onion endpoint, and thirty-five to forty minutes is what it takes. This is the longest onion cook of any documented yassa and the sauce shows it.
Roasting the chicken separately means you get crisp skin, which neither the one-pot nor the grilled version delivers. That is the trade this recipe makes.
Start the onions high, then drop to medium-high. The initial heat drives off the marinade's liquid so the onions can actually colour.
Two onions into the marinade and two sliced for the pan. Keep the split — the blitzed ones become sauce body, the sliced ones keep some texture.
Only five minutes together at the end. Any longer and the roast skin softens, which defeats the method.
Red wine vinegar here against cider vinegar or white vinegar elsewhere. It is a rounder, less sharp acid and it suits the long onion cook.
Vermicelli as a serving option is worth knowing — it is genuinely eaten with yassa in Senegal, not a Western substitution.
commonMistakes: Cooking the onions for fifteen minutes and calling them caramelised.
Roasting the chicken and the onions in the same dish.
Leaving it together too long at the end.
Skipping the slashes in the chicken, so the marinade stays on the surface.

THE DISAGREEMENT WITH SEN014, recorded and not reconciled: that version marinates and then cooks entirely in one pot; this one roasts the chicken separately in a 200C oven while the onions cook down. That version's acid is cider vinegar plus lime; this one's is lemon plus red wine vinegar. This one uses Dijon mustard and olives, which that one does not use at all. Neither is corrected toward the other.

storage: 4 days refrigerated, 3 months frozen. The skin will soften.
reheating: Oven, to recover some of the skin. Covered reheating will not.
healthBenefits: Four onions across four servings is a substantial source of quercetin and prebiotic fibre.
Lemon juice and parsley together supply vitamin C.
Roasting rather than frying keeps the added fat to three tablespoons.
culturalNote: Roasting the chicken apart from the sauce is a restaurant solution to a home-cooking problem — you cannot get crisp skin and a long onion braise out of one pot — and it is the kind of adjustment a chef makes without changing what the dish is.
